note:
v1, COMMON MEASURE: THE EIGHTH SONG, A SKELETON (Harry, 17 Nov about 03:40: "open up 2 new song slots"). The record's fast song: 160, where the other seven run 80 to 138. It is the pair to track 7.
Two guitars have riffs of different lengths: the left one's is 52 sixteenths, the right one's 32 (two bars). Played together they meet again only after 26 bars. Euclid finds what measures two lengths by taking the less from the greater, again and again; this song does that to the riffs. Each section the longer riff is cut down to what was left over, its own tail: 52 against 32, then 20 against 32, 20 against 12, 8 against 12, 8 against 4. Four goes into eight exactly, so four sixteenths, one beat, measures both. Both riffs were written to end on the same beat-long cell, and that cell is where they agree.
- WHAT IS LEFT OVER IS HEARD ALONE: at each cut the band stops and the longer riff plays its tail by itself (20 sixteenths, then 12, 8, 4: the stops get shorter too), and that tail is the next section's riff.
- THE ARGUMENT NARROWS: the bass and the kick go with the shorter riff of each pair, so the rhythm section's cycle shrinks (two bars, a bar and a quarter, three beats, half a bar). From 8 against 12 each riff is one guitar a side; at 8 against 4 the bass and kick drop out and the snare counts every beat, louder and louder; then two beats of nothing.
- THE MEASURE (2:13): every guitar on the one cell, a gallop on the beat, climbing the record's hook notes as chords.
- MEASURED (2:37): now the two riffs can be said together: all the guitars play the long riff four times and the short one four times, in unison.
Track 7 is the cut that has no common measure; this is the finding of one, and it ends on the beat of common time, where the record began.
WHERE THINGS ARE: the short riff alone 0:00, with the band 0:06; 52 against 32 0:12; 20 against 32 0:51; 20 against 12 1:21; 8 against 12 1:43; 8 against 4 2:01; the measure 2:13; measured 2:37; one chord 3:09.

WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen): compscore 68.94 / 72.79 (seeds 0 and 11), the lowest on the record, and the scorer has a point. It hears one timbre (guitars and kit, nothing else yet), one density, and nothing that returns before 2:37. That is what a bare skeleton of this idea is; it is the first thing later rounds owe the song.
- By section the finished file reads -10.2, -9.7, -9.8 for the first three pairs, then -10.7 and -11.8 as it narrows, then -9.1 at the measure: a step of 2.7 dB.
- Against the records every full-band stretch is within 2.5 dB in every band; the commonest gap is 1.3 to 2.3 dB short at 500 Hz-1 kHz and 1 to 2.5 over under 60 Hz (the kick strikes every note of the shorter riff at this speed).
- Each riff is two takes a side (your answer on Common Time's doubling, used here from the start); the two takes are level with each other to 0.2 dB.
- Three versions were benched before this one: the first had no stops and no narrowing and read as one level from 0:06 to 3:09 (64.8).
- The opening is one guitar on the right for six seconds, on purpose: the picture leans right there.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether the cuts can be followed by ear, or whether it is one fast wall with stops in it; whether 160 in sixteenths is tight or a blur on these guitars (nothing else on the record is this fast); whether the two riffs are different enough to tell left from right.
A CARD (one): "Two riffs cut down to one beat: can you follow it?"
NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.
next: Harry's ear on the card (can the cuts be followed). OWED: a second colour (it is guitars and kit only: variety 19), something that returns before 2:37, a lead or a voice for the measure. Then: the two-guitar pairs' mids; whether sixteenths at 160 want a tighter guitar.
